channel.title: Most Fascinating Stories
channel.description: History isn’t defined only by great treaties and epic battles—it turns on the bizarre, the terrifying, and the almost-forgotten coincidences that textbooks left behind. In every episode of Most Fascinating Stories, host Rebecca sets the stage before handing the microphone to a new master storyteller to uncover a true, thoroughly sourced, and dramatized historical event you were never taught in school. Concise 10-to-20 minute deep dives into the unbelievable truths behind humanity’s most famous names and darkest moments.

item.title: Episode 3: Nixon's Midnight Vigil at the Lincoln Memorial
item.description: In May 1970, five days after the Kent State shootings and with Washington D.C. besieged by 100,000 anti-war demonstrators, President Richard Nixon slipped out of the White House unannounced at 4:15 A.M. to speak face-to-face with student protesters at the Lincoln Memorial. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ CHAPTERS: • 00:00 - Intro • 01:00 - Act I: Fortress Washington • 01:47 - Act II: The Sleepless Hours • 03:44 - Act III: Waking Manolo • 05:18 - Act IV: Shadows on the Marble Steps • 07:01 - Act V: The Surreal Dialogue • 10:04 - Conclusion ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ HISTORICAL SOURCES & REFERENCES: • Primary / Archival Record: White House Telephone Logs, Daily Diary of President Richard Nixon, and Secret Service Presidential Detail Logs, May 8–9, 1970; Nixon Presidential Materials, National Archives. • Authoritative Biography / History: H.R. Haldeman, *The Haldeman Diaries: Inside the Nixon White House* (G.P. Putnam's Sons, 1994) & Richard Nixon, *RN: The Memoirs of Richard Nixon* (Grosset & Dunlap, 1978). • Specialized Academic / Institutional Reference: Richard Nixon Presidential Library and Museum, *The Lincoln Memorial Encounter: Oral History Collection*. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ FULL TRANSCRIPT: [Rebecca - Host] Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories, where we uncover the real, well-sourced, and lesser-known tales behind history's most prominent figures. I'm your host, Rebecca. Today, we enter the shadowy corridors of the White House in the turbulent spring of 1970 with President Richard Milhous Nixon. History remembers Nixon in sharp, unforgiving contrasts: the brilliant geopolitical strategist who opened relations with China, and the paranoid politician whose presidency unraveled in the Watergate scandal. He was known for being intensely guarded, aloof, and suspicious of the media and the youth culture of the late sixties. Yet on one bizarre, chilly May night, at the peak of the Vietnam War protests, Richard Nixon did something so shocking, so utterly reckless and unscripted, that his closest advisers believed he had completely lost his mind. Here is George with the full, dramatized story. [George - Storyteller] ACT I: FORTRESS WASHINGTON In early May of 1970, Washington, D.C. felt less like the capital of a democratic republic and more like a city preparing for civil war. Just five days earlier, on May fourth, four unarmed college students had been shot and killed by the Ohio National Guard at Kent State University during protests against Nixon's secret expansion of the Vietnam War into neighboring Cambodia. The nation exploded in fury. Over four hundred colleges and universities shut down in nationwide strikes. Now, on Friday, May eighth, more than one hundred thousand anti-war demonstrators—mostly college students, draft-age men, and young activists—were flooding into the District of Columbia for a massive demonstration on the National Mall. Around the White House, the atmosphere was suffocating. To protect the President from angry crowds, the District government parked dozens of city transit buses bumper-to-bumper around the perimeter fence, forming a giant wall of steel. Inside the adjacent Executive Office Building, troops from the Eighty-Second Airborne Division were bivouacked in the hallways, rifles stacked against marble walls. Inside the Oval Office, Richard Nixon was under siege. He had delivered a tense, combative televised press conference earlier that evening, defending the Cambodian incursion. But behind closed doors, his staff noticed disturbing signs of physical and emotional exhaustion. Nixon had barely slept in forty-eight hours. His eyes were bloodshot; his speech was rapid and disjointed. He was deeply wounded by the hostility directed at him, convinced that the media and the universities were determined to destroy his presidency. [George - Storyteller] ACT II: THE SLEEPLESS HOURS By midnight, the White House grew quiet, but the President could not rest. Nixon retreated to his personal sitting room on the second floor, wearing an old sweater and dress slacks. Between midnight and four in the morning, telephone logs record that Nixon made over fifty phone calls. He called his National Security Advisor Henry Kissinger eight times to re-analyze diplomatic cables. He called his daughter Julie, his press secretary Ron Ziegler, his friend Bebe Rebozo, and various cabinet secretaries, repeating the same anxious question: Did the press conference go well? Did we get our message through? Between calls, Nixon put a recording of Rachmaninoff's Piano Concerto on the phonograph, turning the volume high, pacing the floor. Outside on the National Mall, campfires flickered in the darkness. Thousands of young people, wrapped in sleeping bags and army blankets, were sleeping under the trees, singing peace anthems, preparing for the massive march at sunrise. Nixon walked to the window and stared out into the dark park. An obsession began to form in his restless mind. Why did these young people hate him so fiercely? Why couldn't they see that he wanted peace as much as they did? At four o'clock in the morning, an extraordinary impulse seized him. [George - Storyteller] ACT III: WAKING MANOLO At four-fifteen A.M., Nixon walked down the hall to the bedroom of his personal valet, Manolo Sanchez, a loyal Cuban-American who had served Nixon for years. Nixon knocked on the door and entered. Sanchez sat up in bed, rubbing his eyes in confusion. Manolo, Nixon whispered, have you ever seen the Lincoln Memorial at night? Sanchez blinked, bewildered. No, Mr. President, he replied. Get your clothes on, Manolo, Nixon said with a boyish grin. We are going to go right now. Down in the Secret Service command center, alarm bells went off. Special Agent in Charge Robert Taylor stared in utter disbelief as President Nixon walked into the basement, accompanied only by his valet and his personal physician, Dr. Walter Tkach. Taylor scrambled forward: Mr. President, you can't go out there! The city is packed with demonstrators. We have no advance security! I am going, Bob, Nixon replied calmly, slipping into his heavy blue wool overcoat. Either you come with me, or I'm going alone. Desperate, Taylor rallied three nearby agents. There was no time to organize a motorcade. Nixon, Sanchez, Dr. Tkach, and three stunned Secret Service agents piled into a single unmarked black limousine, slipped through the South Gate, and vanished into the predawn mist. [George - Storyteller] ACT IV: SHADOWS ON THE MARBLE STEPS At four-thirty-five A.M., the black limousine pulled up along Constitution Avenue beneath the towering silhouette of the Lincoln Memorial. A light fog hovered over the Reflecting Pool. Nixon stepped out of the car. With hands thrust deep into his overcoat pockets, the President of the United States began climbing the marble steps into the shadows. Beneath the colossal marble statue of Abraham Lincoln, asleep on the cold stone floor, were about thirty anti-war student demonstrators. They were bundled in sleeping bags, surrounded by acoustic guitars, peace signs, and backpacks. Nixon walked directly into the center of the memorial. He looked up at the statue of Lincoln, then turned to Sanchez, pointing out the carved words of the Second Inaugural Address on the wall: With malice toward none, with charity for all. The sound of leather shoes on marble echoed through the monument. A student from Syracuse University, nineteen-year-old Bob Moustakas, woke up, sat upright, and rubbed his eyes. Standing five feet in front of him, backlit by the monument floodlights, was a man with a sloping nose, heavy jowls, and a familiar dark suit. Moustakas nudged the friend sleeping next to him: Hey... look. Isn't that... Nixon? The friend groaned: You're dreaming, go back to sleep. Nixon smiled, walked over, extended his hand, and said in his deep, unmistakable baritone: Good morning. I'm Richard Nixon. Where are you boys from? [George - Storyteller] ACT V: THE SURREAL DIALOGUE Within minutes, the entire group of students was awake, sitting in their sleeping bags in stunned, paralyzed silence. Word quickly spread down the steps: Nixon is up there! Nixon is at the monument! Dozens more students came sprinting up the marble steps, surrounding the President in the chilly predawn darkness. The Secret Service agents had their hands inside their jackets, gripping their sidearms, terrified that someone would pull a weapon. Instead, an extraordinary, surreal ninety-minute conversation unfolded. Nixon did not scold the students, nor did he hide behind prepared talking points. He spoke in a rambling, stream-of-consciousness style, searching desperately for common human ground. I know you hate the war, Nixon told them, looking into their eyes. I know you think I'm a hawk. But I want peace just as badly as you do. The difference is how we get there. Remember Neville Chamberlain. Appeasement doesn't bring peace; it only brings a bigger war later. He asked the students where they went to school. When one student mentioned Syracuse, Nixon immediately pivoted to football, debating the university's running back strategies. He asked others what they were studying. Then he began talking passionately about the architecture of Prague, the grit of Warsaw, and the spirit of the Russian people. Travel while you're young! Nixon urged them with intense earnestness. Don't let yourselves become bitter! Don't hate! When you hate, you destroy yourself! A female student from California stood up, looked Nixon dead in the eye, and spoke with blunt, devastating clarity: Mr. President, you don't understand us. We don't care about football or monuments or Prague. We care about our friends being killed. We want the killing to stop. Nixon stopped speaking. His shoulders slumped. In the shadows of Lincoln's statue, the President looked at her, nodded slowly, and whispered: I know. I know you do. By six A.M., the sun was cresting the horizon. A crowd of several hundred demonstrators had gathered around the base of the monument, and the mood was turning hostile. Chants of Peace now! began echoing off the marble. Agent Bob Taylor grabbed the President's arm: Mr. President, we have to leave right now. Nixon reluctantly agreed. As he was led down the steps toward the car, a student called out: Thank you for coming, Mr. President! Nixon waved, ducked into the limousine, and sped away. Back at the White House, Chief of Staff H.R. Haldeman woke up to learn that the President had been roaming the National Mall alone in the dark. Haldeman was terrified. When he confronted Nixon in the Oval Office, Nixon was strangely energized, insisting on visiting the empty House of Representatives chamber and then stopping at the Mayflower Hotel for corned beef hash. Haldeman recorded in his diary that night: It was the weirdest day of the entire administration. [Rebecca - Host] CONCLUSION Richard Nixon's predawn vigil at the Lincoln Memorial remains one of the most astonishing moments in American political history. It stripped away all the machinery of state power, revealing a deeply isolated leader who, in a moment of acute national crisis, simply wanted to look his young adversaries in the eye and explain his troubled soul. History rarely affords us such raw, unvarnished glimpses behind the presidential mask. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next time for another forgotten chapter of history. Until then, stay curious.

item.title: Episode 2: Eisenhower and the Hellish 1919 Mud Convoy
item.description: In the summer of 1919, Lieutenant Colonel Dwight D. Eisenhower volunteered for the U.S. Army's first transcontinental motor convoy. Across 3,251 miles of dirt, collapsed bridges, and desert quicksand, the grueling two-month ordeal inspired the modern Interstate Highway System. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ CHAPTERS: • 00:00 - Intro • 00:57 - Act I: The Restless Young Officer • 02:26 - Act II: Departure from the Zero Milestone • 03:55 - Act III: The Quagmires of the Midwest • 05:37 - Act IV: The Desert of Salt and Quicksand • 07:36 - Act V: The Golden Gate and the 37-Year Vision • 09:50 - Conclusion ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ HISTORICAL SOURCES & REFERENCES: • Primary / Archival Record: Dwight D. Eisenhower, *Report on Trans-Continental Trip of the First Motor Transport Brigade*, War Department, Nov 3, 1919; Eisenhower Presidential Library Manuscripts. • Authoritative Biography / History: Stephen E. Ambrose, *Eisenhower: Soldier and Statesman* (Simon & Schuster, 1990). • Specialized Academic / Institutional Reference: U.S. Army Transportation Museum & Federal Highway Administration, *The 1919 Motor Transport Corps Convoy*. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ FULL TRANSCRIPT: [Rebecca - Host] Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories, where we uncover the real, well-sourced, and lesser-known tales behind history's most prominent figures. I'm your host, Rebecca. Today, we turn our gaze to Dwight David Eisenhower. History remembers him as the Supreme Allied Commander who orchestrated the liberation of Europe on D-Day, and as the two-term President who transformed the economic landscape of America by signing the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956. Today, millions of drivers travel seamlessly across the United States on fifty thousand miles of asphalt and concrete, rarely asking where the vision for this colossal highway system came from. The truth is, it was born not in a boardroom or a congressional committee, but in the blinding dust, broken axles, and knee-deep mud of an agonizing, forgotten military expedition in 1919. Here is George with the story. [George - Storyteller] ACT I: THE RESTLESS YOUNG OFFICER In June of 1919, twenty-eight-year-old Lieutenant Colonel Dwight D. Eisenhower was in a foul mood. The First World War had just ended in Europe, and while his West Point classmates like George Patton had earned medals and glory in the trenches of France, young Eisenhower had spent the war stuck in Pennsylvania, commanding a tank training center at Camp Colt. He was an exceptional administrator and a master tactician, but he felt his military career was effectively over. Peacetime was shrinking the army, promotions were frozen, and Eisenhower was desperate for a challenge. That challenge arrived in the form of a bold, unprecedented announcement from the War Department: The United States Army was going to attempt the first transcontinental motorized convoy in American history. They planned to drive a massive military column from Washington, D.C. all the way to San Francisco, California. The purpose was twofold: to test the durability of modern military vehicles under peacetime field conditions, and to thank the American public for their wartime sacrifices through a series of parades across the nation's heartland. Eisenhower immediately volunteered to go as an official observer for the Tank Corps. Along with his close friend Major Sereno Brett, Eisenhower packed his field gear, polished his leather boots, and prepared for what was billed as a triumphant cross-country parade. He had no idea that he was stepping into a sixty-two-day survival trial. [George - Storyteller] ACT II: DEPARTURE FROM THE ZERO MILESTONE On the sunny morning of July seventh, 1919, the convoy assembled at the Zero Milestone on the Ellipse, just south of the White House. The scene was magnificent. Brass bands played patriotic marches; Secretary of War Newton Baker delivered a stirring speech; crowds cheered and waved American flags. Lined up along the street were seventy-nine heavy military vehicles, manned by nearly three hundred soldiers and two dozen officers. There were massive five-ton Class B Liberty trucks, ambulances, light delivery vans, mobile repair trailers, field kitchens, motorcycles with sidecars, and even a colossal six-ton pontoon bridging truck. At precisely eleven-fifteen A.M., engines roared to life, exhaust filled the air, and the great convoy rolled west. For the first few days through Maryland and Pennsylvania, the expedition seemed like a glorious holiday. The Lincoln Highway was paved with asphalt and macadam. The trucks cruised comfortably at twelve to fifteen miles per hour, and in every town, thousands of citizens greeted the soldiers with platters of fried chicken, homemade apple pies, and iced tea. Eisenhower enjoyed the camaraderie, smoking his pipe in the passenger seat of an open staff car. But as soon as the convoy crossed the Ohio River, the paved roads abruptly disappeared. Ahead lay two thousand miles of raw, unpaved American dirt. [George - Storyteller] ACT III: THE QUAGMIRES OF THE MIDWEST In 1919, outside of major cities, American roads were little more than packed-earth wagon trails mapped out in the nineteenth century. And when the convoy hit the Midwest, summer thunderstorms descended with unyielding fury. In Illinois, Iowa, and Nebraska, torrential rains turned the black prairie soil into a bottomless quagmire of thick, gumbo clay. It was not merely mud; it was an adhesive, sucking sludge that clung to wheels like wet cement. Ten-ton cargo trucks sank to their axles within minutes. Their solid rubber tires spun uselessly, digging trenches four feet deep. The convoy ground to a complete standstill. Parade uniforms were quickly abandoned. Eisenhower stripped off his officer's tunic, rolled up his sleeves, and waded into the muck beside the enlisted men. Day after day, under pouring rain, the men worked twelve-hour shifts hauling vehicles out of mud holes using heavy ropes, block and tackle, and tree trunks for leverage. Worse still were the bridges. County road bridges throughout the rural Midwest had been built for horse-drawn wagons carrying a ton of hay, not for heavy steel military trucks weighing eight to ten tons. Time after time, as a Liberty truck rolled onto a wooden trestle bridge, the beams would groan, crack, and collapse into the creek below. The convoy was forced to halt while military engineers cut down nearby trees with two-man saws, rebuilding bridges on the spot just to advance fifty feet. Progress slowed from fifty miles a day to less than fifteen. Men slept in wet blankets by the side of the road, exhausted and covered in grime. [George - Storyteller] ACT IV: THE DESERT OF SALT AND QUICKSAND If the Midwest was a trial by mud, the American West was a trial by fire. By the time the battered convoy reached Wyoming and Utah, the temperature soared over one hundred degrees. The dirt roads of the plains were replaced by blinding alkali dust that penetrated every gasket, carburetor, and soldier's lungs. Radiators boiled over every ten miles. Water was strictly rationed: one canteen per man per day. In late August, the convoy faced its most terrifying hurdle: the Great Salt Lake Desert. Local guides warned them that the southern trail across the salt flats was treacherous, but there was no alternative route. Beneath a thin, brittle crust of dried white salt lay an ocean of soupy, grey quicksand. The heavy trucks broke through the salt crust almost immediately. Within an hour, twelve heavy vehicles were swallowed up to their chassis in burning saline mud. Tires could find no purchase whatsoever. The heat was suffocating. To survive, the soldiers were forced to perform an agonizing labor: they unloaded heavy wooden planks from the supply trucks, carried them forward on foot, laid them beneath the tires, drove the trucks forward twelve feet, picked up the planks from behind, and carried them forward again. For four grueling days, in a blinding expanse of white glare, Eisenhower and his men moved like ants across the desert, advancing at an excruciating pace of less than three miles per hour. Mechanical carnage was everywhere. In his logbook, Eisenhower meticulously recorded the damage: broken fan belts, burned-out clutches, cracked steering knuckles, stripped differentials, and snapped drive shafts. Yet, amidst the exhaustion, Eisenhower marveled at the resilience of the men. Mechanics worked through the night by lantern light, fashioning replacement parts from scrap metal, determined that not a single vehicle would be abandoned. [George - Storyteller] ACT V: THE GOLDEN GATE AND THE 37-YEAR VISION Finally, on September sixth, 1919—sixty-two days after departing the White House—a battered, dented, dust-caked column of trucks rolled down the slopes of the Sierra Nevada, boarded a ferry in Oakland, and arrived in San Francisco. They had covered three thousand two hundred and fifty-one miles in sixty-two days, averaging a miserable five point six miles per hour. They had endured ninety-six major breakdowns, twenty-nine serious vehicle accidents, and had destroyed countless wooden bridges. The official parade in San Francisco was celebrated with medals and banquets, but Eisenhower was deeply troubled. In his formal report to the War Department, the young Lieutenant Colonel issued a stark and prophetic warning: The road network of the United States was utterly primitive and completely incapable of supporting military movement. If a foreign adversary launched an amphibious invasion of either the Atlantic or Pacific coast, the United States Army could not even transport troops and supplies across its own continent to defend the nation. The lesson burned into Eisenhower's soul. A quarter of a century later, General Eisenhower stood in Europe as Supreme Commander, watching Allied armies race across Germany on the modern, divided Reichsautobahn. He immediately connected the dots back to the summer of 1919 in the Utah mud. In 1953, when Eisenhower was inaugurated as the thirty-fourth President of the United States, fixing America's broken roads became one of his highest personal priorities. On June twenty-ninth, 1956, President Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act, launching a twenty-five-billion-dollar initiative to construct forty-one thousand miles of high-speed, controlled-access interstate highways—the largest public works project in human history. Today, that system bears his name: the Dwight D. Eisenhower National System of Interstate and Defense Highways. Whenever we drive at seventy miles an hour across the American heartland, we are traveling on a vision forged in the sweat, grit, and mud of a young soldier who spent two months pushing broken trucks out of the desert sand. [Rebecca - Host] CONCLUSION Eisenhower's 1919 convoy is a powerful testament to how personal hardship can shape national destiny. Without those sixty-two miserable days in the Midwest mud, the Interstate Highway System that connected modern America might never have been built. It proves that sometimes, the greatest forward strides begin with a broken axle. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next time for another forgotten chapter of history. Until then, stay curious.

item.title: Episode 1: FDR and the Friendly Torpedo That Almost Killed Him
item.description: In November 1943, President Franklin D. Roosevelt embarked on a top-secret transatlantic voyage aboard the battleship USS Iowa to meet Churchill and Stalin in Tehran. During live combat exercises, an escort destroyer accidentally launched an armed torpedo directly at the President's ship. Hosted by Rebecca, with story narration by George. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ CHAPTERS: • 00:00 - Intro • 00:47 - Act I: The Cursed Escort • 02:36 - Act II: Depth Charges in the Storm • 04:01 - Act III: Balloons and Blue Skies • 05:16 - Act IV: Fire Two: The Runaway Torpedo • 06:33 - Act V: Wheel Me to the Railing • 08:42 - Act VI: Under Arrest in Bermuda and the Pardon • 10:38 - Conclusion ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ HISTORICAL SOURCES & REFERENCES: • Primary / Archival Record: Deck Logs of USS Iowa (BB-61) & USS William D. Porter (DD-579), 12–14 Nov 1943; Records of the Bureau of Naval Personnel, National Archives RG 24. • Authoritative Biography / History: James MacGregor Burns, *Roosevelt: The Soldier of Freedom 1940–1945* (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1970). • Specialized Academic / Institutional Reference: Naval History and Heritage Command, *USS William D. Porter (DD-579) Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships*. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ FULL TRANSCRIPT: [Rebecca - Host] Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories, where we uncover the real, documented, and lesser-known tales behind history's most prominent figures. I'm your host, Rebecca. Today, we step into the stormy autumn of nineteen forty-three with President Franklin Delano Roosevelt. We remember FDR for his fireside chats, the New Deal, and steering the Allied powers through World War Two. But history often turns on absurd, razor-thin margins. In November of nineteen forty-three, on a voyage shrouded in total wartime secrecy, an American warship accidentally fired a live, fully armed torpedo directly at the battleship carrying the Commander-in-Chief. And now, here is George with the story. [George - Storyteller] ACT I: THE CURSED ESCORT In the second week of November nineteen forty-three, a thick, cold fog blanketed the waters off Hampton Roads, Virginia. Sliding quietly out into the Atlantic under the cloak of night was the mightiest warship in the United States Navy: the newly commissioned battleship USS Iowa. She was an eighty-eight-thousand-horsepower fortress of steel, carrying nine sixteen-inch guns and armor plates over a foot thick. Aboard was a passenger whose presence was the most closely guarded secret of the war: President Franklin D. Roosevelt. Accompanied by Army Chief of Staff George C. Marshall, Admiral Ernest King, and his closest diplomatic advisers, Roosevelt was embarking on Operation Sextant, crossing the Atlantic to meet Winston Churchill in Cairo and Joseph Stalin in Tehran. It was to be the first face-to-face summit of the Big Three leaders, a meeting that would decide the timing of D-Day and the postwar partition of Europe. For security against German U-boat wolfpacks that infested the Atlantic sea lanes, the Iowa was surrounded by a protective screen of cruisers and destroyers. Among these escorts was a fresh Fletcher-class destroyer: hull number five-seven-nine, the USS William D. Porter, commanded by Lieutenant Commander Wilfred Walter. To her crew of mostly green recruits, the Porter was their ticket to glory. But from the moment she pulled out of Norfolk, the ship seemed cursed with astonishing misfortune. While maneuvering away from the dock, the Porter's stern anchor had hooked onto the railing of a neighboring sister destroyer, ripping away stanchions, railings, and a lifeboat before freeing herself. Captain Walter had delivered a stern dressing-down to his young crew, hoping that humiliating mishap would be their last. It was only the prelude. [George - Storyteller] ACT II: DEPTH CHARGES IN THE STORM Twenty-four hours into the voyage, the convoy ran into ferocious North Atlantic seas. The wind whipped up towering whitecaps, and the destroyers rolled violently in the heavy ocean swells. Suddenly, a massive underwater explosion shook the entire ocean. A thunderous shockwave hammered against the hull of the Iowa. Aboard the battleship, sirens wailed into the storm: General Quarters! Gun crews sprinted to their battle stations; lookout binoculars swept the gray horizons; the Iowa's massive turbines surged to life, heeling the ship into violent zigzag maneuvers. German U-boats were presumed to be attacking the President's flagship. Depth-charge crews stood ready on all destroyers, scanning the foaming waves for periscopes. But there were no German submarines in sight. Minutes later, a shamefaced signal flashed across the water from the William D. Porter. An improperly secured depth charge had rolled off her stern rack during a heavy wave roll and detonated upon reaching its pressure depth. Admiral Ernest King was apoplectic. To broadcast an accidental depth-charge explosion in the middle of the Atlantic was like lighting a flare for every Nazi submarine within a hundred miles. Captain Walter was reprimanded via blinker light, and the men of the Porter hung their heads in disgrace. They desperately needed an opportunity to prove their competence. [George - Storyteller] ACT III: BALLOONS AND BLUE SKIES The opportunity seemed to arrive on Sunday, November fourteenth. The convoy was cruising east of Bermuda, and the weather had cleared into brilliant sunshine and calm blue seas. President Roosevelt, wearing his trademark fedora and clutching a long cigarette holder between his teeth, was brought onto the Iowa's teakwood deck in his wheelchair. He loved the sea; as a former Assistant Secretary of the Navy, Roosevelt was in his element. To entertain the Commander-in-Chief, the Iowa's captain arranged an anti-aircraft gunnery demonstration. Crewmen released large silver weather balloons high into the cloudless sky. Moments later, the Iowa's five-inch, forty-millimeter, and twenty-millimeter guns opened up in a roaring symphony of fire, shredding the silver balloons into ribbons. FDR smiled broadly, puffing his cigarette and applauding the gunnery. Across six thousand yards of open water, Captain Walter of the William D. Porter watched the demonstration. Here was his chance to redeem his ship in the eyes of the President and the high command. Walter ordered his crew to conduct a simulated torpedo drill, using the distant, colossal silhouette of the Iowa as their mock target. [George - Storyteller] ACT IV: FIRE TWO: THE RUNAWAY TORPEDO On the Porter's deck, the torpedo mount was manned by Torpedoman Third Class Lawton Dawson. In a live-fire combat situation, the Mark fifteen torpedoes carried eighteen hundred pounds of high explosives. For a dry drill, Navy regulations strictly mandated that the small explosive primer charges used to expel the torpedoes from their tubes must be removed. Dawson removed the primers from tubes one and three. But on tube number two, in the excitement and noise of the exercise, he made a catastrophic oversight: he left the primer in place. On the bridge, Captain Walter shouted the standard drill command: Mount two, stand by! Fire two! Instead of a hollow metallic click, a terrifying whoosh echoed across the deck. An exhaust plume of white compressed gas billowed into the air. Before the horrified eyes of the crew, a two-ton, fully armed, live torpedo splashed into the Atlantic, its propeller screaming to life at forty-five knots, churning a deadly white frothy wake heading straight for the Iowa. Utter chaos engulfed the bridge of the William D. Porter. Captain Walter stared in disbelief, turning pale as chalk. A live torpedo was speeding directly toward the President of the United States. [George - Storyteller] ACT V: WHEEL ME TO THE RAILING They had less than two minutes before impact. Strict radio silence was in effect to conceal the mission from Axis listening stations. Desperate to warn the Iowa without breaking radio protocols, Walter ordered his signalman to flash an urgent warning with the Aldis lamp. The signalman, shaking with adrenaline, aimed the lamp at the Iowa's towering bridge and began frantically clacking the shutter. Torpedo in water, steer right! he intended to say. Instead, in his blinding panic, the signalman transposed letters. What the Iowa's lookouts read was: Porter is backing up full speed! Aboard the Iowa, the bridge crew blinked in irritation. They flashed back: Porter, clarify message. Seeing that visual signals were failing, Captain Walter threw naval regulations out the window. He grabbed the TBS radio microphone, broke radio silence, and screamed over the fleet's open frequency: Lion, lion, come right! Hard right! Lion, look right! Torpedo in the water! Inside his stateroom, President Roosevelt felt the violent lurch of the deck. Secret Service agent Mike Reilly rushed into the room, shouting that a torpedo was inbound. Most leaders would have ducked for cover inside the conning tower. But Roosevelt's eyes lit up with intense curiosity. Wheel me to the railing, Mike, Roosevelt insisted. I want to see it! Reilly wheeled the President out onto the deck to the starboard railing. With his fedora firmly on his head, Franklin Roosevelt watched the foaming silver track of the torpedo race across the Atlantic directly toward his ship. At the very last moment, the Iowa's sharp evasive turn paid off. The torpedo sliced through the water, missing the stern by roughly twelve hundred yards, detonating in the churning wake. A magnificent geyser of white foam and saltwater erupted hundreds of feet into the sky. The concussion shook the deck of the Iowa, spraying fine ocean mist onto Roosevelt's face. The President let out a low chuckle, removed his cigarette holder, and turned to his aides with a grin. [George - Storyteller] ACT VI: UNDER ARREST IN BERMUDA AND THE PARDON Aboard the Iowa's bridge, however, nobody was smiling. Admiral King and Captain McCrea were utterly convinced they had just survived an assassination plot. Suspicion immediately fell upon the William D. Porter. The Iowa swiveled all nine of her massive sixteen-inch turrets—guns capable of firing twenty-seven-hundred-pound armor-piercing shells twenty miles—and locked them squarely onto the diminutive destroyer. The Porter was ordered to stand down, surrender its logs, and report directly to naval authorities in Bermuda under armed escort. Upon arriving in Bermuda, Marines boarded the William D. Porter and placed the entire crew—officers, sailors, and cooks alike—under military arrest. It was the only time in United States naval history that an entire ship's company was arrested en masse. Interrogations were fierce. Naval intelligence combed through every crewman's background, searching for German saboteurs. Finally, Lawton Dawson, weeping in remorse, confessed that he had inadvertently left the primer in tube number two, and in his panic, had thrown the spent primer casing overboard to hide his mistake. Dawson was court-martialed and sentenced to fourteen years of hard labor. But when the verdict reached the Oval Office, President Roosevelt intervened personally. Writing to the Secretary of the Navy, FDR stated that no harm had been done, that it was clearly an accident born of training frenzy, and asked that Dawson be pardoned and restored to duty. The Navy complied, but they never quite forgave the Porter. The destroyer was exiled to the frozen, fog-choked outpost of the Aleutian Islands. For the remainder of the war, whenever the William D. Porter pulled into a naval anchorage, other American ships would hail her over the radio with the same sardonic joke: Don't shoot, boys, we're Republicans! [Rebecca - Host] CONCLUSION The saga of the William D. Porter remains one of the most astonishing near-misses in modern history. Had that torpedo struck the Iowa's magazine, the course of World War Two—the timing of the cross-channel invasion, the atomic bomb program, and the entire architecture of the postwar world—would have been radically altered in a single blinding flash. Roosevelt's unflappable calm at the railing, asking to be wheeled closer to watch the weapon approach, captures the indomitable spirit of a leader who refused to let fear dictate his life. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next time as we unearth another forgotten chapter from the pages of history. Until then, stay curious.
